text: Once you've written the same three lines a second time, it's time for a function. Data work is full of small repeated operations: add tax to a price, clean a name, flag a large order. A function gives that operation a name so you can reuse it, test it, and read it. A comprehension is Python's compact way of building a new list, dictionary, or set from an existing one, and you'll see it in nearly every piece of data code you read from here on.

A function starts with def, a name, parameters in parentheses, and an indented body; return sends a value back to the caller. Define add underscore tax with a price and a rate that defaults to 0.08. Call it with just a price and you get 54.0; pass rate equals 0.10 by name and you get 55.0 instead. That default means the caller can omit the rate entirely, and naming an argument like rate equals 0.10 makes the call easier to read, especially once a function has several parameters.

A function can return more than one value — Python packs them into a tuple you unpack on the spot. Define order underscore stats to return the min, the max, and the average of a list of totals in one line; call it and unpack straight into lo, hi, and avg, getting 8.25, 130.0, and 53.44. A short description inside triple quotes on the first line of the body, called a docstring, lets tools show that description as help text later.

A common beginner mistake is forgetting return entirely. A function without one still runs, but hands back None — the computed value gets thrown away the moment the function ends. Define no underscore return to compute x times 2 but never return it; call it with 3, and the result you get back is None, not 6, because the doubling happened and then vanished.

Here's the loop version of apply tax to every total: an empty list, a for loop appending add underscore tax of each item. And here's the comprehension version — one line that says the same thing: with underscore tax equals add underscore tax of t, for t in totals. Read it as 'an add-tax of t for each t in totals.' The general shape is expression, for item in items, with an optional if at the end that filters which items are kept — big equals t for t in totals if t is greater than 20.

To choose between two values for each item, put a conditional expression at the front, before the for: 'big' if t is greater than 50 else 'small', for t in totals. Notice the difference — an if at the end filters items out, while an if-else at the front transforms every single item. The same idea works with curly braces for a dictionary: strip and title-case each messy name as the key, its stripped length as the value, giving a clean lookup in one line.

Keep comprehensions short — if one needs more than about one line of thinking, a regular loop is the kinder choice for the next reader. A lambda is a one-expression function with no name, most useful as a key argument when sorting. Sort a list of name-amount pairs by the amount, using a lambda that picks out the second element, with reverse equals True for largest first. You'll meet this exact pattern again in pandas, applying small functions to columns.

To recap: def names a piece of logic, defaults make parameters optional, and forgetting return quietly gives back None. A comprehension is expression, for item in items, with an optional if condition; dict comprehensions use key-colon-value for the same loop; and lambda covers tiny one-off functions, especially for sorting. Next lesson: the core data structures — lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets.
